name: Chef D.'s Lishush Mush
subtitle: Everything soft. Nothing simple.
description:
The name is the menu and the menu is a pronunciation guide. Chef Delilah Rishrush has no teeth and has never regarded this as a limitation, and the whole establishment is built on the proposition that texture is the least interesting thing food can offer.

Inside, the room is exactly the right size. It is exactly the right size when there are two diners and it is exactly the right size when there are thirty, and nobody has ever had to wait and nobody has ever eaten in an echo. The walls are a colour that changes its mind about being a colour. There are eleven tables tonight. You have counted eleven every time and you have never seen the same eleven.

And the air. Somebody has done something to the air in here, and what they have done to it is: it tastes.
revisit:
Chef D. has your order going before the door has finished swinging. She does not ask for an order and she has never asked for one, and in eleven years what has arrived has not once been wrong, and the one time you tried to order something else she made that as well and put both down and said nothing about it.

The pass is loud. T is doing something at the far end that involves a great deal of knife and no visible attention. The extraction fan is running, and it will go quiet in a moment, and neither of them will remark on that either.

lucid.2: The onomatopoeia she cooks by is not describing the food. It is keeping time with something.
lucid.3: Under the extraction fan there is a sound with pauses in it, and Chef D. cooks in the pauses and rests in the striking.
lucid.4: She is not cooking to a rhythm. She is cooking in the gaps, the way a person talks in the gaps when somebody else is talking.

ambient: A diner puts down a spoon, looks at the middle distance for four seconds with an expression of mild and pleasant recognition, and picks the spoon back up. Whatever arrived was not unwelcome. Whatever arrived was also not theirs.

T comes out of the kitchen, delivers eleven seconds of soliloquy on the subject of a root vegetable to a room that is largely eating, receives no response whatsoever, and goes back in entirely satisfied.

The colour of the wall commits to being green, thinks better of it, and settles on something it can defend at a committee. Nobody in the room looks up. The couple nearest the wall go on with their conversation against a colour that is now three shades warmer than the one they sat down in front of.
Chef D. laughs at something T says through the pass. It is a big unguarded laugh from a face with nothing behind it to protect, and it stops the room for about a second, and the room is glad of it.
Something on the stove says *shhhk*, once, and Chef D. moves toward it without looking, arriving exactly when she needs to.

objects.name: the menu
objects.description:
Hand-lettered, laminated, and — this is the establishment's central and only complaint, and it is never made aloud — unstable.

You read: TOMORROW'S MEMORIES SEARED IN YESTERDAY'S REGRETS. You order it, by pointing, because pointing feels safer. What arrives is described by the person carrying it as something else entirely: a different dish, in a different register, with a different number of words in the name.

You go back to the menu to establish which of you is wrong.

The menu is on your side of the argument. Not blank, not changed — it agrees with what you now believe you read, and it does so in a way that makes it perfectly clear you must have misremembered a moment ago, and the laminate is unscratched and the lettering is unmistakably hand-done and years old.

This has happened to every diner in this room. It is not discussed, in the specific way that a thing which happens to everybody and can be verified by nobody is never discussed.
objects.repeat: You have started reading it aloud, quietly, as a control. It does not help. The words come out of your mouth in one order and are on the card in another by the time your eye returns to them, and the laminate is unmarked, and the lettering is unmistakably hand-done.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the menu is a list of eleven dishes and it is completely stable. Every one is crossed out. Underneath, in a hand that is not Chef D.'s and is not steady, somebody has written eleven replacements — and then crossed those out too, and then written the first eleven back.

passive.text: The menu is not changing. If it were changing you would catch it changing, because you have been watching it. It is your *account* of the menu that is being brought into line with the menu, retroactively, and the menu is being kept as the fixed point.
'Tomorrow's Memories Seared in Yesterday's Regrets' is not a dish name. It is a working title, and a bad one, and somebody knows it is bad, which is why it does not survive to the plate.

clue.title: You are what gets revised
clue.text: The Lishush Mush menu does not change; the diner's memory of it is brought into line afterwards. The menu is kept as the fixed point.

clue.title: Crossed out, replaced, restored
clue.text: Under the monocle every dish on the menu is crossed out, replaced in an unsteady hand that is not Chef D.'s, and then the originals are written back.

check.prompt: Your account of the menu is being revised while you are not looking at it, which means the revision has to happen in the gap. Catch the gap. Look away and back faster than the revision can be made.
check.success:
You catch the tail of it. For a quarter of a second the laminate holds two dish names in the same place, one fading under the other, and the one fading is the one you read and the one arriving is the one you will remember reading.

The correction is not on the menu. It is on you, and you have just watched it be applied.
check.failure: TOMORROW'S MEMORIES SEARED IN YESTERDAY'S REGRETS. You look away and back and it says something else and has always said something else, and the something else is not interesting.

clue.title: The correction is applied to you
clue.text: Caught mid-revision, the Lishush Mush menu holds two names at once — and the edit is being made to the reader rather than the board.

objects.name: the liver and onions
objects.description:
It arrives without being ordered, as it has arrived without being ordered on every visit — and Chef D.'s position on this, delivered toothlessly, warmly, and without any apparent sense that it requires defending, is that a man named Onions who has not been given onions has been failed by his restaurant.

It is soft. Everything here is soft; there is not a tooth in the kitchen and the whole menu has been built around that fact by somebody who decided long ago that it was a constraint rather than a tragedy.

It is also, and this is not a matter of opinion or of mood, extraordinary. The liver tastes of something that has no business being a taste — something in the region of a long afternoon, in a warm house, where somebody in the next room is painting and has not spoken for a while and does not need to.

The onions are arranged on top. Ten rings, then nine, then seven, and one long piece laid across the whole of it.

They arrange themselves further while you are looking at the plate.
objects.repeat: Four rows again. You have started counting the rounds in each row before you pick up the fork, the way a man checks a stair he already knows will hold, and it has been ten, nine, seven and a long one every single time.

lucid.2: Four rows. Ten, nine, seven, and a long one at the bottom that your thumb wants to press.
lucid.4: It is a keyboard. It has been a keyboard every time, on your plate, in front of you, going cold while you failed to look at it.

objects.monocle: Through the gold the onions are keys. Not like keys — keys, with the little dished tops and the wire linkages going down into the liver, and the long one at the bottom is a space bar, and one of the keys in the top row is worn shinier than the others, and it is the O.

passive.text: Ten, nine, seven, and a long one. Anybody who has ever sat in front of a machine knows that shape without having to be told it.
It is going cold while you conduct an investigation into its layout. Eat it. It is the best thing that will happen to you today and it is not getting better.

clue.title: Ten, nine, seven, and a long one
clue.text: The unordered liver and onions arranges itself into four rows of evenly spaced rounds — ten, nine, seven, and a long one at the bottom.

clue.title: The O is worn shiny
clue.text: Under the monocle the onions are typewriter keys with linkages going down into the liver. One key in the top row is worn shinier than the rest. It is the O.

check.prompt: The onions rearrange while you look at them, which means they do not rearrange while you look at them. Look faster than the rearrangement, and do not blink at the wrong moment.
check.success:
You catch it mid-move. Ten, nine, seven and a long one — and for the half-second before it settles, the arrangement is *not* four rows of onions. It is four lines of type, set and waiting, and one of the lines is longer than the others because it has a name in it.

Then it is onions, and it is very good, and the plate is warm.
check.failure: Ten, nine, seven, and a long one. You look away and back and it is ten, nine, seven, and a long one, and the rearranging happens exactly and only in the place where you are not.

clue.title: Four lines of type
clue.text: Caught mid-move, the onions on the liver resolve into four set lines of type, the last one longer because it contains a name.

objects.name: the health inspector's file
objects.description:
Antopolis Ficklefuk comes on Thursdays. He has come on Thursdays for nine years without missing one, and he keeps the most meticulous records in Silvora Reefs, and he keeps them in a hand so regular that the pages look printed until you get close.

The file lives in a wire rack by the door, because the regulations state that it must be available for inspection. Nobody has ever inspected it except you. You have now done so four times, and the file has not been moved between visits, and the dust on the rack has not been disturbed by anybody but you.

The observations column is exhaustive and entirely without editorial. *Room dimension at 1904h: 6.2m. Room dimension at 1911h: 9.4m. No structural work observed. No personnel present at wall.* *Dish served under name not appearing on menu. Menu subsequently correct.* *Utensil aloft, unsupported, 4s, kitchen. Sous chef speaking at time of observation.*

The findings column, on every page, for nine years, in the same steady hand, says: NO MATTERS ARISING.
objects.repeat: Two new Thursdays on the file. Utensil aloft, six seconds. Diner reports temporal displacement, mild, no complaint. Signed, dated, filed, and the file goes back behind the pass where anybody could read it and nobody ever has.
objects.monocle: Through the gold, NO MATTERS ARISING is a stamp and not a signature, and the stamp has four lobes, and it has been applied to the findings column *before* the observations column was filled in. The ink of the finding is under the ink of the observation on every page for nine years.

passive.text: He is not covering it up. A man covering it up would not write it down. He is doing something much stranger: recording it in full and then certifying that nothing happened, in the same document, in the same hand.

Nine years of Thursdays. He measures the room twice a visit because measuring it twice is the only part of this that is his. Somebody told him what the findings column would say a long time ago, and he has been filling the other column ever since out of self-respect.

clue.title: NO MATTERS ARISING
clue.text: Nine years of health inspections at Lishush Mush record dimensional changes, unsupported utensils and non-existent dishes in exhaustive detail. Every findings column reads NO MATTERS ARISING.

clue.title: The finding was stamped first
clue.text: Under the monocle, NO MATTERS ARISING is a four-lobed stamp applied before the observations were written. The ink of the conclusion lies under the ink of the evidence on every page for nine years.

check.prompt: The file is behind the pass and the kitchen is busy and Chef D. is entirely capable of noticing a man going where he should not. Get to it without being the sort of guest who gets to it.
check.success:
There is a half-second every ninety seconds when the pass is loud and nobody is facing the shelf. You take it in that half-second and read it standing up and put it back in the next one.

Nine years. Every findings column reads NO MATTERS ARISING — and on the last page, this Thursday, in a different hand: *matters arising*, lower case, unstamped, unfinished.
check.failure: You get the file off the shelf and Chef D. says your name — the one she uses, which is 'love' — from four feet away without turning round, and asks whether you are hungry, and you put it back and say yes.

clue.title: matters arising
clue.text: The last page of the inspector's file, this Thursday, in a different hand and unstamped: 'matters arising', lower case, unfinished.

objects.name: the Can't Elope Antelope
objects.description:
It is on the menu and it is on the menu at every establishment in Silvora Reefs that has ever wanted to annoy Woolbinkle, which is all of them.

Here it is served in a bowl, soft, pale, and it is the only dish in the room that arrives looking different to each person at the table. You have watched this happen. Four diners, one dish, four honest descriptions, no two overlapping, and a general table-wide agreement afterwards that it had been very good.

Chef D. will tell you, if you ask, that she does not know what is in it. She will tell you this cheerfully and it is not a joke and it does not trouble her. Her position is that she cooks it correctly and the ingredients are between the dish and the diner.
objects.repeat: Different again. You are getting better at not describing it to yourself while it is in front of you, which helps, and which is the most disquieting sentence you have formed this week.
objects.monocle: Through the gold, the bowl contains one word, and the word is CANNED, and it has been canned.

check.prompt: Eat it. Everything in this room has been extraordinary and this is the thing the room is named for, and there is no version of tonight in which you leave without having tried it.
check.success:
Soft. Warm. And then a taste that is not a taste but a *held note*, low, sustained, the way an organ holds a chord under a hymn — and while the note is held, a great deal of Silvora Reefs is briefly available to you at once, the way a town is available from a hill.

You are aware of Rest Assured, and the count of its vaults, which is nineteen. You are aware of Darek's back hallway, which is eleven feet. You are aware of a small room with a green lamp in it, which is nine by eleven, and which is not in Silvora Reefs, and which is nonetheless the room all of the others are measured from.

Then it is a bowl of something soft, and Chef D. is saying *shhhk* at a pan, and your spoon is halfway to your mouth and has been for some time.
check.failure:
Soft. Warm. Extraordinary. And nothing else — no note, no hill, no town laid out.

At the bottom of the bowl there is a single round of cantaloupe, which is not an ingredient in anything else in this room, and which sits there being a joke told by somebody who is not present and who has been waiting a long time for you to reach the bottom of a bowl.

clue.title: The room everything is measured from
clue.text: Under the Can't Elope Antelope, the whole town becomes briefly available at once — and every measurement in it resolves against a small green-lamped room, nine feet by eleven, which is not in Silvora Reefs.

clue.title: A round of cantaloupe
clue.text: At the bottom of the bowl, one round of cantaloupe — an ingredient in nothing else in the building, and a joke told by somebody not present.

objects.name: the arrangement on the plate
objects.description:
Chef D. puts them down the same way every time and has never once been asked about it, because it is a garnish, and nobody in the history of eating has interrogated a garnish.

Ten rings. Then nine. Then seven. Then one long piece, laid across the whole of it at a slight angle, always last.

Always that. Always in that order, always the long one last, and she does it without looking at the plate — her hands go to three places on the board and the fourth cut is longer, every time, without measuring, while she is talking to you about something else entirely.

The rings are not the same size as each other within each group, which rules out a mould and rules out habit-of-the-knife. They are placed. Each one is put where it goes, and the spacing between the groups is wider than the spacing within them, and it is wider by about the same amount every time.
objects.repeat: Ten, nine, seven, and a long one. She has served you eleven times and it has been ten, nine, seven and a long one on all eleven plates, laid down in that order, the long one last, without her once looking at what her hands were doing.
objects.monocle: Through the gold the rings are not rings. They are strokes, and they are being written left to right by somebody in a hurry to get it down before the plate goes out.

passive.text: She does not look at the plate while she does it. Her hands go to the same three places on the board and the fourth cut is longer, every time, without measurement.

clue.title: Ten, nine, seven, and a long one
clue.text: Chef D. arranges the onions identically on every plate — ten rings, nine, seven, and one long piece across — without looking, and has never been asked about it.

check.prompt: It is not a garnish. Garnishes vary, and this one has not varied in eleven visits. Stop looking at it as food and work out what it is a picture of.
check.success:
Count them as counts and they are nothing. Look at them as *shapes on a surface*, from above, in the order she lays them, and they resolve the way a word resolves when the handwriting stops being handwriting.

Three groups and a crossbar. Ten, nine, seven — and then the long one laid across all three, which is the stroke you put through a word when you have written it out and it is finished.

She cannot say the sounds. She has had no teeth for thirty years and there are letters that will not survive her mouth, and she has been setting them down in onion, on a plate, several times a night, for as long as anybody in this parish can remember — and then striking them out and sending them into the room to be eaten.
check.failure: Ten, nine, seven, a long one. It stays a garnish. It is a very good garnish and it goes well with the liver, and Chef D. watches you look at it and says nothing about it, which she has been doing for years and is extremely good at.

clue.title: She has been writing it down
clue.text: The onions are strokes, not rings — three groups and a crossbar, a word written and then struck out. Chef D. has no teeth and there are sounds she cannot make, so she sets them on a plate several times a night and sends them out to be eaten.

exits.outside_inn: back down toward the water, and a building with weather in it
exits.cheeses_thrice: along the narrow street, toward an oven and a great deal of feeling
exits.gs_spot: a corner you will not be able to point to afterwards
